Question Paper  
Exam Date & Time: 21-Dec-2025 (09:30 AM - 12:30 PM)  
  
  
  MANIPAL ACADEMY OF HIGHER EDUCATION  
  MANIPAL INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY - BENGALURU  
  SEVENTH SEMESTER B.TECH. DEGREE MAKEUP EXAMINATIONS - DECEMBER 2025  
  Social Network Analysis [NPT_4146]  
Marks: 50                                                                                                    Duration: 180 mins.  
  
  PART-A  
Answer all the questions.  
  
1)                Consider the following code snippet and answer the questions below:                                     (5)  
  
  
  A)           import networkx as nx  
  $$G = nx.Graph()$$  
  G.add_nodes_from(["Rahul", "Sneha", "Amit", "Priya", "Karan"])  
  G.add_edges_from([("Rahul", "Sneha"), ("Rahul", "Amit"), ("Sneha", "Priya"), ("Amit", "Karan")])  
  G.remove_edge("Rahul", "Amit")  
  G.remove_node("Priya")  
  $$has_edge = G.has_edge("Rahul", "Amit")$$  
  $$neighbors_of_rahul = list(G.neighbors("Rahul"))$$  
  
  Apply and interpret how the application of remove_edge(), remove_node(), has_edge(), and  
  neighbors() functions modifies the underlying social network structure. Further, evaluate the  
  resulting network connectivity and construct an extended version of the graph by adding a new  
  connection between Sneha and Karan. Explain how this modification influences the relationships  
  among the remaining individuals.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO1" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
  B)           Apply graph metrics such as betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and modularity in             (3)  
  Gephi to analyze and interpret the key structural properties of a network. Examine how these  
  metrics reveal influential nodes and community structures, and illustrate their computation and  
  visualization within the software.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO1" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
  C)           Apply the concept of betweenness centrality to analyze and interpret the role of intermediary           (2)  
  nodes in facilitating information flow within large, real-world networks such as social media  
  platforms. Examine how variations in betweenness values reflect node influence and discuss the  
  implications of these findings for understanding key connectors in the network.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO1" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
2)                Consider a node v in a social network. This node has 4 neighbors: A, B, C, and D. The                   (5)  
  connections between these neighbors are as follows:  
  A)  
  A is connected to B and C.  
  B is connected to C.  
  C is connected to D.  
  
  Analyze the local clustering coefficient of node v in the given social network with neighborsA, B, C,  
  Page #1

and D, considering the specified interconnections among the neighbors, and interpret what the  
  resulting value reveals about the cohesiveness of node v's neighborhood.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO2" / Cognitive Level: "Analysis"  
  
  B)   The following table represents a social network of six individuals with their attributes and           (3)  
  friendships:  
  
  
  Examine the given network to identify two instances of homophily-cases where friendships occur  
  between individuals sharing the same gender or occupation. Discuss what these patterns indicate  
  about the tendency of people to form connections based on shared attributes in social  
  networks.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO2" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
  C)   Apply the concept of social influence in network analysis to determine who-Alice with 200       (2)  
  connections or Bob with 50 connections-would likely have a greater impact when sharing the same  
  post, and justify your reasoning based on network connectivity principles.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO2" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
3)        Apply the concept of network isolation to explain how spatial segregation leads to the formation       (5)  
  of isolated clusters within a network, and interpret the implications this has for information flow,  
  A)   access to diverse perspectives, and social mobility in society  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO3" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
  B)   The following table represents the relationships among five individuals in a small social group:       (3)  
  Relationship     Type of Relationship  
  A-B              Positive (+)  
  A-C              Negative (-)  
  B-C              Positive (+)  
  B-D              Negative (-)  
  C-E              Positive (+)  
  D-E              Negative (-)  
  Examine the network using the concept of balance theory by identifying the total number of positive  
  and negative relationships and determining which single relationship adjustment would achieve  
  balance.  
  Page #2

Course Outcome: "CO3" / Cognitive Level: "Analysis"  
  
  C)         Utilize the concept of balance theory to explain how changing one negative relationship to a positive (2)  
  one can transform an unstable triad into a stable configuration in a social network.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO3" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
4)              Examine the limitations of using power-law distributions to model real-world social networks.          (5)  
  Identify key criticisms related to how well the power-law model fits empirical network data, and  
  A)         analyze how researchers can address these challenges when interpreting or validating social  
  network structures.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO4" / Cognitive Level: "Analysis"  
  
  B)         Analyze how the "richer gets richer" effect (preferential attachment) influences the degree            (3)  
  distribution of a social network and results in the formation ofhighly influential nodes.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO4" / Cognitive Level: "Analysis"  
  
  C)         Apply the concept of the long-tail phenomenon in a degree distribution within the context of Social    (2)  
  Network Analysis, and explain what it reveals about the presence of a few highly connected nodes  
  and many sparsely connected nodes in the network.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO4" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
5)              Utilize the mathematical foundations of the small-world model and explain six degrees of               (5)  
  separation, viral marketing, information diffusion in real-world applications.  
  A)  
  Course Outcome: "CO5" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
  B)         Apply the cascading model to explain the process of information diffusion, highlighting how            (3)  
  information spreads progressively from one user to others within a social network.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO5" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
  C)         Utilize the concept of short path lengths to examine how information or viral content quickly          (2)  
  propagates through a social network.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO5" / Cognitive Level: "Application"  
  
  
  -----End-----
